title: Jesse Owens and Luz Long in Berlin
text:
At the Berlin Olympics in August 1936, staged by the Nazi regime as a display of Aryan supremacy, the American sprinter Jesse Owens entered the long jump. In qualifying he fouled on his first two attempts and was one jump from elimination.

In the version Owens told for decades afterward, the German jumper Luz Long came over, introduced himself and suggested that Owens mark a spot well before the takeoff board and jump from there to be safe. Owens qualified easily. In the final the two fought a duel; Owens won with 8.06 meters and Long took silver. Long was the first to congratulate him, and the two walked arm in arm around the stadium in front of the German crowd.

They wrote to each other after the Games. Long was killed in Sicily in 1943 while serving in the German army. According to Owens, Long had written asking him, if he died, to look up his son and tell him about his father. Owens later met the son, Kai, and remained close to the Long family. Long was posthumously awarded the Pierre de Coubertin Medal for sportsmanship.
lesson: Treat a rival as a fellow human being, whatever the politics around you. Sportsmanship and friendship across a hostile divide can outlast the regimes that tried to forbid them.
source: Jesse Owens with Paul Neimark, The Jesse Owens Story (1970); Jeremy Schaap, Triumph (2007)
caveat: The advice during qualifying comes only from Owens's later accounts and has been questioned; the friendship and the embrace after the final are well attested.
